questions.explanation: send a link 概括 submit...for possible inclusion；提交内容是 blog。
questions.distractorAnalysis: travels 是博客记录的内容，不是被提交收录的载体；website 是收录平台。

questions.prompt: The website www.newzealand.com aimed to provide ready-made itineraries and packages for travel companies and individual tourists.
questions.promptZh: www.newzealand.com 旨在为旅游公司和个人游客提供现成的行程与套餐。
questions.evidence: The website was set up to allow both individuals and travel organisations to create itineraries and travel packages to suit their own needs and interests.
questions.explanation: 网站让用户自行 create 并按自身需要定制，不是由网站 provide ready-made 成品；核心动作相反。
questions.distractorAnalysis: TRUE 被 travel organisations/individuals 与 itineraries/packages 的词汇重合诱导；NOT GIVEN 不成立，因为原文明确说明创建方式。

questions.prompt: It was found that most visitors started searching on the website by geographical location.
questions.promptZh: 研究发现，大多数访客在网站上最先按地理位置进行搜索。
questions.evidence: visitors can search for activities not solely by geographical location, but also by the particular nature of the activity
questions.explanation: 原文只列出两种可用搜索维度，没有说明 most visitors 的实际行为，也没有说明 started searching 的先后。
questions.distractorAnalysis: FALSE 需要原文明确否定“大多数先按地点搜索”，但 not solely 只是说功能不止一种；TRUE 同样缺少使用数据。

questions.prompt: According to research, 26% of visitor satisfaction is related to their accommodation.
questions.promptZh: 研究表明，游客满意度的26%与住宿有关。
questions.evidence: transport and accommodation account for the remaining 26%
questions.explanation: 26% 是 transport 与 accommodation 合计占比，题干把合计范围缩成 accommodation 单项，构成范围矛盾。
questions.distractorAnalysis: TRUE 会忽视并列项 transport；NOT GIVEN 不成立，因为原文给出了明确但范围不同的百分比。

questions.prompt: Visitors to New Zealand like to become involved in the local culture.
questions.promptZh: 到新西兰的游客喜欢亲身参与当地文化。
questions.evidence: visitors enjoy cultural activities most when they are interactive, such as visiting a marae (meeting ground) to learn about traditional Maori life
questions.explanation: become involved 对应 interactive，local culture 对应 traditional Maori life；原文明确说这种互动文化活动最受喜欢。
questions.distractorAnalysis: FALSE 与 enjoy...most 直接冲突；NOT GIVEN 忽视了 marae 的具体例证。

questions.prompt: Visitors like staying in small hotels in New Zealand rather than in larger ones.
questions.promptZh: 游客在新西兰更喜欢住小型酒店，而不是大型酒店。
questions.evidence: New Zealand is a small country with a visitor economy composed mainly of small businesses.
questions.explanation: 原文只说旅游经济以小企业为主，没有比较游客对小型与大型酒店的住宿偏好。
questions.distractorAnalysis: TRUE 是把 small businesses 偷换成 small hotels 并虚构偏好；FALSE 也无反向偏好证据。

questions.prompt: Many visitors feel it is unlikely that they will return to New Zealand after their visit.
questions.promptZh: 许多游客觉得，此次旅行后他们不太可能再回到新西兰。
questions.evidence: what is often seen as a once-in-a-lifetime visit
questions.explanation: once-in-a-lifetime 表示一生大概只有一次，蕴含访客认为再次到访可能性很低。
questions.distractorAnalysis: NOT GIVEN 会忽略该固定表达的语义推断；FALSE 与 often seen as a once-in-a-lifetime visit 相反。

questions.promptZh: A段
questions.evidence: But defining boredom so that it can be studied in the lab has proved difficult. For a start, it can include a lot of other mental states... There isn’t even agreement...
questions.explanation: 本段中心不是定义无聊本身，而是说明实验室研究首先卡在定义与边界不统一，因此选 iv。

questions.promptZh: B段
questions.evidence: ...identified five distinct types... These can be plotted on two axes...
questions.explanation: 五种类型加两条坐标轴构成一套分类系统，选 vi。

distractorAnalysis.i: 本段只评价类型，不谈创造性成果。
distractorAnalysis.viii: 末句只提出未来研究问题，不是本段中心。

questions.promptZh: C段
questions.evidence: Mann has found that being bored makes us more creative... a passive, boring activity is best for creativity...
questions.explanation: 实验和结论都指向无聊带来创造力这一积极产出，选 i。

distractorAnalysis.iii: 主旨是好处，不是解释加疗法。

questions.promptZh: D段
questions.evidence: ...it can still be toxic if allowed to fester... repeatedly failing to engage attention can lead to a state where we don’t know what to do any more, and no longer care.
questions.explanation: 段落从无聊的适应性转向其毒性及注意力反复失败的危险后果，选 v。

distractorAnalysis.i: Eastwood反对把走神创造力等同于无聊。
distractorAnalysis.iv: 不是在讨论实验定义问题。

questions.promptZh: E段
questions.evidence: Boredom proneness has been linked with a variety of traits... People who are motivated by pleasure... curiosity... a high boredom threshold.
questions.explanation: 本段先用人格特质识别谁更容易无聊，再补充后果与应对，中心是易感人群，选 viii。

distractorAnalysis.i: 未把创造性成果作为中心。
distractorAnalysis.ii: 青少年研究不等于教师措施。
distractorAnalysis.iii: 只有应对建议，没有新解释加新疗法的完整组合。
distractorAnalysis.v: 虽提危险，但为易感性后果，不是组织中心。
distractorAnalysis.vii: teenagers是研究对象，不是年龄组比较。

questions.promptZh: F段
questions.evidence: ...our over-connected lifestyles might even be a new source of boredom... leave our phones alone, and use boredom to motivate us to engage with the world in a more meaningful way.
questions.explanation: 过度连接是新解释，放下手机并借无聊重新投入世界是新应对，两个部分正对应 iii。

questions.promptZh: 彼得·图希
questions.evidence: If disgust protects humans from infection, boredom may protect them from “infectious” social situations...
questions.explanation: protect...from 与 idea E 的 encourage us to avoid 构成同义改写。

distractorAnalysis.C: 原文无人提出未来下降。

questions.promptZh: 托马斯·格茨
questions.evidence: Of the five types, the most damaging is ‘reactant’ boredom...
questions.explanation: the most damaging 精确对应 worse than all the others。

questions.promptZh: 约翰·伊斯特伍德
questions.evidence: What’s more, your efforts to improve the situation can end up making you feel worse.
questions.explanation: efforts to improve 对应 trying to cope，feel worse 对应 increase negative effects。

questions.promptZh: 弗朗索瓦丝·韦梅尔斯费尔德
questions.evidence: ...our over-connected lifestyles might even be a new source of boredom.
questions.explanation: over-connected lifestyles 与 the way we live today 同义，new source 对应 encourage boredom。

questions.prompt: people cannot 24 ______, due to a failure in what he calls the ‘attention system’
questions.promptZh: 由于所谓“注意力系统”失灵，人们无法______
questions.evidence: This causes an inability to focus on anything...
questions.explanation: cannot 后接动词原形；原文 inability to focus 直接改写为 cannot focus。ONE WORD ONLY，不能写 focus on。

distractorAnalysis.engage: 后文是 engage attention，不直接对应 cannot 后的中心能力表述。
distractorAnalysis.attention: 词性不合，cannot 后需动词。
distractorAnalysis.concentrate: 语义可通但不是原文词。

questions.prompt: those for whom 25 ______ is an important aim in life may have problems in coping with boredom
questions.promptZh: 把______视为人生重要目标的人可能难以应对无聊
questions.evidence: People who are motivated by pleasure seem to suffer particularly badly.
questions.explanation: motivated by pleasure 被改写为 pleasure is an important aim；空格需名词，答案为原文单词 pleasure。

distractorAnalysis.personality: 范围过大，原文明确指出具体动机。
distractorAnalysis.motivation: 不是原文对应目标的词。
distractorAnalysis.satisfaction: 虽语义相关，但不是证据句用词。

questions.prompt: those who have the characteristic of 26 ______ can generally cope with it
questions.promptZh: 具有______这一特质的人通常能应对无聊
questions.evidence: Other personality traits, such as curiosity, are associated with a high boredom threshold.
questions.explanation: high boredom threshold 表示较能承受无聊；characteristic of 后接名词，原文为 curiosity。

distractorAnalysis.threshold: 它是结果指标，不是人的特质内容。
distractorAnalysis.curious: 词性不合，of 后此处需要名词且必须取原文一词。

questions.prompt: What is the writer suggesting about computer-produced works in the first paragraph?
questions.promptZh: 作者在第一段对计算机创作的作品作出了什么暗示？

options.A: People’s acceptance of them can vary considerably.
options.B: A great deal of progress has already been attained in this field.
options.C: They have had more success in some artistic genres than in others.
options.D: The advances are not as significant as the public believes them to be.

questions.evidence: Classical music by an artificial composer has had audiences enraptured ... Artworks painted by a robot have sold for thousands of dollars ... And software has been built which creates art that could not have been imagined by the programmer.
questions.explanation: 三个并列实例分别说明机器音乐能打动并欺骗听众、机器人画作进入名贵画廊、软件甚至能产生程序员未预想到的艺术，合起来强调该领域已取得大量进展。

distractorAnalysis.A: 段中列举不同成果，不是在比较公众接受度的波动。
distractorAnalysis.C: 没有比较不同艺术门类谁更成功。
distractorAnalysis.D: 作者强调成果显著，并未说公众高估进步。

questions.prompt: According to Geraint Wiggins, why are many people worried by computer art?
questions.promptZh: 根据 Geraint Wiggins 的说法，为什么许多人担忧计算机艺术？

options.A: It is aesthetically inferior to human art.
options.B: It may ultimately supersede human art.
options.C: It undermines a fundamental human quality.
options.D: It will lead to a deterioration in human ability.

questions.evidence: They are worried that it is taking something special away from what it means to be human.
questions.explanation: “从身为人类的意义中拿走某种特殊之物”对应“削弱一种根本的人类特质”。

distractorAnalysis.A: Wiggins 没有评价机器艺术审美低劣。
distractorAnalysis.B: 没有说机器艺术最终会取代人类艺术。
distractorAnalysis.D: 担忧指向人类独特性的定义，而非人的能力退化。

questions.prompt: What is a key difference between Aaron and the Painting Fool?
questions.promptZh: Aaron 与 Painting Fool 的关键区别是什么？

options.A: its programmer’s background
options.B: public response to its work
options.C: the source of its subject matter
options.D: the technical standard of its output

questions.evidence: Aaron ... is still little more than a tool to realise the programmer’s own creative ideas. Unlike earlier ‘artists’ such as Aaron, the Painting Fool only needs minimal direction and can come up with its own concepts by going online for material.
questions.explanation: Aaron 的题材与创意来自程序员；Painting Fool 会联网取材并形成自己的概念，差异在题材来源。

distractorAnalysis.A: 文中没有比较两位程序员的背景。
distractorAnalysis.B: 未把公众反应作为两者差别。
distractorAnalysis.D: 没有比较输出的技术水准。

questions.prompt: What point does Simon Colton make in the fourth paragraph?
questions.promptZh: Simon Colton 在第四段提出了什么观点？

options.A: Software-produced art is often dismissed as childish and simplistic.
options.B: The same concepts of creativity should not be applied to all forms of art.
options.C: It is unreasonable to expect a machine to be as imaginative as a human being.
options.D: People tend to judge computer art and human art according to different criteria.

questions.evidence: Colton argues that such reactions arise from people’s double standards towards software-produced and human-produced art. ... ‘The same should be true of a machine.’
questions.explanation: 核心词是 double standards：人们用不同标准判断机器艺术与人类艺术。

distractorAnalysis.A: 文中只说有些人觉得画面机械，并非幼稚简单。
distractorAnalysis.B: Colton 主张同一想象力标准也应适用于机器，恰与本项相反。
distractorAnalysis.C: 他没有降低对机器想象力的期待，而是在要求公平判断。

questions.prompt: The writer refers to the paintings of a chair as an example of computer art which
questions.promptZh: 作者提及椅子画，是把它作为哪一类计算机艺术的例子？

options.A: achieves a particularly striking effect.
options.B: exhibits a certain level of genuine artistic skill.
options.C: closely resembles that of a well-known artist.
options.D: highlights the technical limitations of the software.

questions.evidence: Some of the Painting Fool’s paintings of a chair came out in black and white, thanks to a technical glitch. This gives the work an eerie, ghostlike quality.
questions.explanation: 技术故障意外带来“诡异、幽灵般”的鲜明效果，因此选 A。

distractorAnalysis.B: 作者描述效果，没有据此认定真正艺术技巧。
distractorAnalysis.C: Ellsworth Kelly 只是被用来作公平标准的类比，不是说画作与他相似。
distractorAnalysis.D: 故障是成因，但段落强调它产生的艺术效果，而非软件局限。

questions.prompt: Simon Colton says it is important to consider the long-term view when
questions.promptZh: Simon Colton 说，在何种情况下应当采取长远眼光？

options.A: generating work that was virtually indistinguishable from that of humans.
options.B: knowing whether it was the work of humans or software.
options.C: producing work entirely dependent on the imagination of its creator.
options.D: comparing the artistic achievements of humans and computers.
options.E: revealing the technical details of his program.
options.F: persuading the public to appreciate computer art.
options.G: discovering that it was the product of a computer program.

questions.evidence: Researchers like Colton don’t believe it is right to measure machine creativity directly to that of humans who ‘have had millennia to develop our skills’.
questions.explanation: “人类已有数千年发展技能”要求在比较人机艺术成就时采用长期尺度，故 D。

distractorAnalysis.A: 这是 EMI 的惊人表现，对应第 33 题。
distractorAnalysis.B: 这是 Moffat 实验的盲测条件，对应第 37 题。
distractorAnalysis.C: 这是 Hofstadter 对 EMI 的批评，对应第 35 题。
distractorAnalysis.E: 这是 Wiggins 指责 Cope 未做之事，对应第 34 题。
distractorAnalysis.F: 文中没有说 Colton 的长远观点用于说服公众。
distractorAnalysis.G: 这是听众愤怒的触发因素，对应第 36 题。

questions.prompt: David Cope’s EMI software surprised people by
questions.promptZh: David Cope 的 EMI 软件以何种表现令人大吃一惊？

options.A: generating work that was virtually indistinguishable from that of humans.
options.B: knowing whether it was the work of humans or software.
options.C: producing work entirely dependent on the imagination of its creator.
options.D: comparing the artistic achievements of humans and computers.
options.E: revealing the technical details of his program.
options.F: persuading the public to appreciate computer art.
options.G: discovering that it was the product of a computer program.

questions.evidence: EMI even fooled classical music experts into thinking they were hearing genuine Bach.
questions.explanation: 连古典音乐专家都误以为是真正的巴赫，说明作品与人类作品几乎无法区分，故 A。

distractorAnalysis.B: EMI 不是判断作者身份的主体。
distractorAnalysis.C: 这是批评而非令人惊讶的成就。
distractorAnalysis.D: EMI 没有进行人机成就比较。
distractorAnalysis.E: Cope 恰被批评没有披露技术细节。
distractorAnalysis.F: 没有说软件主动劝服公众。
distractorAnalysis.G: 发现机器身份的是听众，对应第 36 题。

questions.prompt: Geraint Wiggins criticised Cope for not
questions.promptZh: Geraint Wiggins 批评 Cope 没有做什么？

options.A: generating work that was virtually indistinguishable from that of humans.
options.B: knowing whether it was the work of humans or software.
options.C: producing work entirely dependent on the imagination of its creator.
options.D: comparing the artistic achievements of humans and computers.
options.E: revealing the technical details of his program.
options.F: persuading the public to appreciate computer art.
options.G: discovering that it was the product of a computer program.

questions.evidence: Wiggins ... condemned him for his deliberately vague explanation of how the software worked.
questions.explanation: “故意含糊地解释软件原理”就是没有公开程序的技术细节，故 E。

distractorAnalysis.A: Wiggins 的批评不是作品不像人类。
distractorAnalysis.B: 与 Cope 是否知道创作者身份无关。
distractorAnalysis.D: 没有要求 Cope 比较人机成就。
distractorAnalysis.F: 没有批评他未劝服公众。
distractorAnalysis.G: 不是要求 Cope 发现作品来源。

questions.prompt: Douglas Hofstadter claimed that EMI was
questions.promptZh: Douglas Hofstadter 声称 EMI 是怎样的？

options.A: generating work that was virtually indistinguishable from that of humans.
options.B: knowing whether it was the work of humans or software.
options.C: producing work entirely dependent on the imagination of its creator.
options.D: comparing the artistic achievements of humans and computers.
options.E: revealing the technical details of his program.
options.F: persuading the public to appreciate computer art.
options.G: discovering that it was the product of a computer program.

questions.evidence: EMI created replicas which still rely completely on the original artist’s creative impulses.
questions.explanation: replicas 且 completely rely on 原艺术家的创意冲动，等于作品完全依赖其创作者的想象力，故 C。

distractorAnalysis.A: 这是 EMI 欺骗专家所显示的表面相似度，不是 Hofstadter 的批评重点。
distractorAnalysis.B: 不是 EMI 在辨认作品来源。
distractorAnalysis.D: 他没有说 EMI 比较成就。
distractorAnalysis.G: 发现机器来源的是听众。

questions.prompt: Audiences who had listened to EMI’s music became angry after
questions.promptZh: 听过 EMI 音乐的听众在发生什么之后变得愤怒？

options.A: generating work that was virtually indistinguishable from that of humans.
options.B: knowing whether it was the work of humans or software.
options.C: producing work entirely dependent on the imagination of its creator.
options.D: comparing the artistic achievements of humans and computers.
options.E: revealing the technical details of his program.
options.F: persuading the public to appreciate computer art.
options.G: discovering that it was the product of a computer program.

questions.evidence: When audiences found out the truth they were often outraged with Cope.
questions.explanation: truth 指音乐由程序生成；得知这一来源后听众才愤怒，故 G。

distractorAnalysis.A: 作品像人类作品原本让人感动，并非生气的时间触发点。
distractorAnalysis.B: 不是“知道是否”，而是明确发现来自软件。
distractorAnalysis.C: 听众并非因依赖创作者想象力而怒。

questions.prompt: The participants in David Moffat’s study had to assess music without
questions.promptZh: David Moffat 研究中的参与者必须在不知道什么的情况下评价音乐？

options.A: generating work that was virtually indistinguishable from that of humans.
options.B: knowing whether it was the work of humans or software.
options.C: producing work entirely dependent on the imagination of its creator.
options.D: comparing the artistic achievements of humans and computers.
options.E: revealing the technical details of his program.
options.F: persuading the public to appreciate computer art.
options.G: discovering that it was the product of a computer program.

questions.evidence: The participants weren’t told beforehand whether the tunes were composed by humans or computers, but were asked to guess, and then rate how much they liked each one.
questions.explanation: 参与者事先不知道曲子由人还是计算机创作，故 B。

distractorAnalysis.A: 不是参与者自己生成作品。
distractorAnalysis.C: 不是评价前被隐瞒的具体信息。
distractorAnalysis.D: 他们评价曲目，不是直接比较人机历史成就。
distractorAnalysis.E: 与 Cope 程序细节无关。
distractorAnalysis.F: 参与者没有承担劝服公众的任务。
distractorAnalysis.G: G 表示已经发现是程序产品，与“without knowing”相反。

questions.prompt: Moffat’s research may help explain people’s reactions to EMI.
questions.promptZh: Moffat 的研究或许有助于解释人们对 EMI 的反应。

options.NOT GIVEN: the writer’s view is impossible to determine

questions.evidence: But why did so many people love the music, yet recoil when they discovered how it was composed? A study by computer scientist David Moffat ... provides a clue.
questions.explanation: 作者先提出听众得知来源后反感之谜，紧接着说 Moffat 的研究“provides a clue”，明确支持题干。

distractorAnalysis.NO: 原文不是否认解释力，而是说研究提供线索。
distractorAnalysis.NOT GIVEN: 作者已明确表达研究与反应之间的解释关系。

questions.prompt: The non-experts in Moffat’s study all responded in a predictable way.
questions.promptZh: Moffat 研究中的非专家全都以一种可预测的方式作出了反应。

options.NOT GIVEN: the writer’s view is impossible to determine

questions.evidence: People who thought the composer was a computer tended to dislike the piece more ... This was true even among the experts.
questions.explanation: 原文只给总体倾向，并说专家中也有这一倾向；没有说明非专家是否“全都”如此，也没有评价其反应是否可预测。

distractorAnalysis.YES: tended to 不能推出 all，也没有 predictable。
distractorAnalysis.NO: 原文同样没有明确说非专家并非全部如此，因此不能判 NO。

questions.prompt: Justin Kruger’s findings cast doubt on Paul Bloom’s theory about people’s prejudice towards computer art.
questions.promptZh: Justin Kruger 的研究结果使 Paul Bloom 关于人们对计算机艺术偏见的理论受到质疑。

options.NOT GIVEN: the writer’s view is impossible to determine

questions.evidence: he reckons part of the pleasure we get from art stems from the creative process behind the work. ... experiments by Justin Kruger ... have shown that people’s enjoyment of an artwork increases if they think more time and effort was needed to create it.
questions.explanation: Kruger 发现人们认为创作投入越多便越享受作品，正好支持 Bloom 所说愉悦部分源于创作过程，因此题干“cast doubt”与原文相反。

distractorAnalysis.YES: 两项观点是相互支持，不是质疑。
distractorAnalysis.NOT GIVEN: 原文并列呈现两者，并清楚显示逻辑一致，足以判断为 NO。

SAMPLE ANSWER
This is an answer written by a candidate who achieved a Band 6.5 score. Here is the
examiner's comment:
The candidate deals with both parts of the prompt and addresses some social and
practical problems that might be experienced in a foreign language environment.
Ideas are supported by examples, though there is room for further development
here. Organisation is logical and there is clear progression throughout the
response. Cohesive devices are used appropriately [Another problem | For
example | Therefore | That means ... | The second ... problem | To summarize].
There is a sufficient range of vocabulary to allow some flexibility and precision and
to demonstrate awareness of style and collocation [language barrier linked to
influence the behaviour | offend | misunderstanding | misconceptions]. There is a
mix of simple and complex sentence forms including subordinate clauses [which
means that | a person who], modal verbs [should | might | would] and gerunds
[finding a job]. Grammatical control is generally good as is the use of punctuation,
although the first sentence in the second paragraph is incomplete.
It is clear that living in a foreign country has its own benefits and drawbacks to consider. I agre
with this statement, however I think that anybody coming in another country should respect national
culture. In this essay, I would like to outline the social and practical problems.
The social problems would be language barrier, which means that a person coming from another
country might not be able to speak and understand the language which might be a problem as far
a person who is living in a country, and a person who came in the country. Another problem is
linked to the language barrier, but it might influence the behaviour of others. An individual who
come into the country might offend others with their behaviour or language. For example; some
cultures like English people prefer to be very polite and say things differently from other cultures.
Therefore a person who doesn't know how to behave in a particular culture might offend others
around him.
The practical problems would be misunderstanding of culture. That means that a person who visits
other countries does not understand other culture and he behaves as he wants to.
The second practical problem is finding a job. An individual who works in foreign country might not
be appropriate for people who he serves. For example if an individual works in a restaurant, the
people who live in a country and they were born in that country might not respect and not like the
behaviour of a person who works in a restaurant, it might be because, the cultures are different.
To summarize, it can be said that there are a lot of misconceptions which people have when they
come in a foreign country, and in my opinion and from my personal experience people should
educate themselves in order to know how to behave in different situations with different cultures.

Sample answers for Writing tasks
TEST 1, WRITING TASK 1
SAMPLE ANSWER
This is an answer written by a candidate who achieved a Band 5.5 score. Here is the
examiner's comment:
The candidate has identified all the key features (hospital, ring road, new public
car park, staff car park and bus station in 2010) but the descriptions are not always
accurate e.g. [two features that still remained. This two features are City Hospital
and staff car park] whereas the staff car park was formerly a car park for both staff
and public, while the mention of the bus station is not developed. Organisation is
clear, however, with some good use of cohesive devices [According to  Apart from
The further additional features], although there is an error in the use of reference
pronouns [This/These two features]. The range of vocabulary is sufficient for the
task [two different years | features | remained | additional], though [features] is
over-used. A spelling error is noted in the second line [sourrounded] but this
does not cause any difficulty for the reader; similarly, the use of [around-turn]
can be easily understood as 'roundabout'. There is a mix of simple and complex
sentences, mainly used accurately.
Two maps illustrate the way to get to a city hospital of two different years (2oo7 and 2010).
According to both maps, the main features which is city hospital is sourrounded by Ring Road. In
these two maps, there have been two features that still remained. This two features are City Hospital
and staff car park. Apart from these two features there are some features that shows on 2olo map
but haven't shown on 2007 map. The additional features that appear on the map of 2010 are public
car park which located on the east-side of the city hospital. The further additional features are two
around-turn on the hospital Rd. which can lead to the bus station.
Overall, there are two major features that never change on both 2007 and 2010 map. These features
are city hospital and staff car park. However, there are some additional features that appear
on the map of 2oio but not on 2oo7. These features are public car park, bus station and two
around-turns.
126

Sample answers for Writing tasks
TEST 1, WRITING TASK 2
SAMPLE ANSWER
This is an answer written by a candidate who achieved a Band 6.5 score. Here is the
examiner's comment:
The candidate deals with both parts of the prompt and addresses some social and
practical problems that might be experienced in a foreign language environment.
Ideas are supported by examples, though there is room for further development
here. Organisation is logical and there is clear progression throughout the
response. Cohesive devices are used appropriately [Another problem | For
example | Therefore | That means ... | The second ... problem | To summarize].
There is a sufficient range of vocabulary to allow some flexibility and precision and
to demonstrate awareness of style and collocation [language barrier linked to
influence the behaviour | offend | misunderstanding | misconceptions]. There is a
mix of simple and complex sentence forms including subordinate clauses [which
means that | a person who], modal verbs [should | might | would] and gerunds
[finding a job]. Grammatical control is generally good as is the use of punctuation,
although the first sentence in the second paragraph is incomplete.
It is clear that living in a foreign country has its own benefits and drawbacks to consider. I agre
with this statement, however I think that anybody coming in another country should respect national
culture. In this essay, I would like to outline the social and practical problems.
The social problems would be language barrier, which means that a person coming from another
country might not be able to speak and understand the language which might be a problem as far
a person who is living in a country, and a person who came in the country. Another problem is
linked to the language barrier, but it might influence the behaviour of others. An individual who
come into the country might offend others with their behaviour or language. For example; some
cultures like English people prefer to be very polite and say things differently from other cultures.
Therefore a person who doesn't know how to behave in a particular culture might offend others
around him.
The practical problems would be misunderstanding of culture. That means that a person who visits
other countries does not understand other culture and he behaves as he wants to.
The second practical problem is finding a job. An individual who works in foreign country might not
be appropriate for people who he serves. For example if an individual works in a restaurant, the
people who live in a country and they were born in that country might not respect and not like the
behaviour of a person who works in a restaurant, it might be because, the cultures are different.
To summarize, it can be said that there are a lot of misconceptions which people have when they
come in a foreign country, and in my opinion and from my personal experience people should
educate themselves in order to know how to behave in different situations with different cultures.
127

TEST 2, WRITING TASK 2
SAMPLE ANSWER
This is an answer written by a candidate who achieved a Band 7.0 score. Here is the
examiner's comment:
The candidate explains why s/he both agrees and disagrees with the statement,
meeting the requirements of 'To what extent do you agree or disagree with this
statement?' S/he singles out two areas of disagreement (food and jobs) and
provides clear examples to support these opinions, then goes on to identify an area
of agreement (TV channels), again providing support and then some development
of the example. Organisation is logical and there is clear progression throughout
the writing. There is a range of cohesive devices, used appropriately [Take for
example | Actually | Therefore | Naturally | However | This specific area | From this
point of view In conclusion]. The range of vocabulary is sufficient to show some
flexibility and precision, as well as less common items and an awareness of style
and collocation [Complex | list of favourites | fits ... my abilities | specific area
many available channels]. There is only one spelling error [beome], probably a slip
of the pen. Control over grammar and punctuation is generally good and there is a
variety of complex structures with frequent error-free sentences.
The answer is complex since there are a lot of choices in our life and all of them are different
kinds. In some cases I would say that it is a good thing to have the ability to choose from a wide
variety. Take for example gastronomy. Every single person has different meals on their list of
favourites. Actually if you have a bigger family it is almost impossible to cook something that
everyone would like. Therefore I would say that it is great that you can go to a shopping center and
choose from a dozen different food types. I can always find something that looks delicious.
Naturally, there are some people who say that it is against evolution. They claim to say that back in
the old days we had a perfect life when technically everybody was farming. I personally disagree with
that. I am happy that I could choose a job that fits best to my abilities. I mean no one is the same,
why would we want to do the same? Different kinds of universities give us the opportunity to beome
who we are meant to be. We have the right to choose.
However there is one topic where, according to my opinion, we have too many choices. This specific
area is television. There are hundreds of channels, therefore you can always find something that
is worth watching. Literally you could sit in your sofa the whole day and watch films. I think that
people doing less outdoor activities are the results of the many available channels. From this point
of view I would agree that we have too many choices.
In conclusion I would say that we can't generally talk about choices since they could be different. In
some cases it is good to have many of them while in other areas they could have a negative effect.

tests.title: Cambridge IELTS 13 Reading Test 2
tests.passage:
Cinnamon is a sweet, fragrant spice produced from the inner bark of trees of the genus Cinnamomum, which is native to the Indian sub-continent. It was known in biblical times, and is mentioned in several books of the Bible, both as an ingredient that was mixed with oils for anointing people’s bodies, and also as a token indicating friendship among lovers and friends. In ancient Rome, mourners attending funerals burnt cinnamon to create a pleasant scent. Most often, however, the spice found its primary use as an additive to food and drink. In the Middle Ages, Europeans who could afford the spice used it to flavour food, particularly meat, and to impress those around them with their ability to purchase an expensive condiment from the ‘exotic’ East. At a banquet, a host would offer guests a plate with various spices piled upon it as a sign of the wealth at his or her disposal. Cinnamon was also reported to have health benefits, and was thought to cure various ailments, such as indigestion.

Toward the end of the Middle Ages, the European middle classes began to desire the lifestyle of the elite, including their consumption of spices. This led to a growth in demand for cinnamon and other spices. At that time, cinnamon was transported by Arab merchants, who closely guarded the secret of the source of the spice from potential rivals. They took it from India, where it was grown, on camels via an overland route to the Mediterranean. Their journey ended when they reached Alexandria. European traders sailed there to purchase their supply of cinnamon, then brought it back to Venice. The spice then travelled from that great trading city to markets all around Europe. Because the overland trade route allowed for only small quantities of the spice to reach Europe, and because Venice had a virtual monopoly of the trade, the Venetians could set the price of cinnamon exorbitantly high. These prices, coupled with the increasing demand, spurred the search for new routes to Asia by Europeans eager to take part in the spice trade.

Seeking the high profits promised by the cinnamon market, Portuguese traders arrived on the island of Ceylon in the Indian Ocean toward the end of the 15th century. Before Europeans arrived on the island, the state had organized the cultivation of cinnamon. People belonging to the ethnic group called the Salagama would peel the bark off young shoots of the cinnamon plant in the rainy season, when the wet bark was more pliable. During the peeling process, they curled the bark into the ‘stick’ shape still associated with the spice today. The Salagama then gave the finished product to the king as a form of tribute. When the Portuguese arrived, they needed to increase production significantly, and so enslaved many other members of the Ceylonese native population, forcing them to work in cinnamon harvesting. In 1518, the Portuguese built a fort on Ceylon, which enabled them to protect the island, so helping them to develop a monopoly in the cinnamon trade and generate very high profits. In the late 16th century, for example, they enjoyed a tenfold profit when shipping cinnamon over a journey of eight days from Ceylon to India.

When the Dutch arrived off the coast of southern Asia at the very beginning of the 17th century, they set their sights on displacing the Portuguese as kings of cinnamon. The Dutch allied themselves with Kandy, an inland kingdom on Ceylon. In return for payments of elephants and cinnamon, they protected the native king from the Portuguese. By 1640, the Dutch broke the 150-year Portuguese monopoly when they overran and occupied their factories. By 1658, they had permanently expelled the Portuguese from the island, thereby gaining control of the lucrative cinnamon trade. In order to protect their hold on the market, the Dutch, like the Portuguese before them, treated the native inhabitants harshly. Because of the need to boost production and satisfy Europe’s ever-increasing appetite for cinnamon, the Dutch began to alter the harvesting practices of the Ceylonese. Over time, the supply of cinnamon trees on the island became nearly exhausted, due to systematic stripping of the bark. Eventually, the Dutch began cultivating their own cinnamon trees to supplement the diminishing number of wild trees available for use.

Then, in 1796, the English arrived on Ceylon, thereby displacing the Dutch from their control of the cinnamon monopoly. By the middle of the 19th century, production of cinnamon reached 1,000 tons a year, after a lower grade quality of the spice became acceptable to European tastes. By that time, cinnamon was being grown in other parts of the Indian Ocean region and in the West Indies, Brazil, and Guyana. Not only was a monopoly of cinnamon becoming impossible, but the spice trade overall was diminishing in economic potential, and was eventually superseded by the rise of trade in coffee, tea, chocolate, and sugar.

Oxytocin is a chemical, a hormone produced in the pituitary gland in the brain. It was through various studies focusing on animals that scientists first became aware of the influence of oxytocin. They discovered that it helps reinforce the bonds between prairie voles, which mate for life, and triggers the motherly behaviour that sheep show towards their newborn lambs. It is also released by women in childbirth, strengthening the attachment between mother and baby. Few chemicals have as positive a reputation as oxytocin, which is sometimes referred to as the ‘love hormone’. One sniff of it can, it is claimed, make a person more trusting, empathetic, generous and cooperative. It is time, however, to revise this wholly optimistic view. A new wave of studies has shown that its effects vary greatly depending on the person and the circumstances, and it can impact on our social interactions for worse as well as for better.

Oxytocin’s role in human behaviour first emerged in 2005. In a groundbreaking experiment, Markus Heinrichs and his colleagues at the University of Freiburg, Germany, asked volunteers to do an activity in which they could invest money with an anonymous person who was not guaranteed to be honest. The team found that participants who had sniffed oxytocin via a nasal spray beforehand invested more money than those who received a placebo instead. The study was the start of research into the effects of oxytocin on human interactions. ‘For eight years, it was quite a lonesome field,’ Heinrichs recalls. ‘Now, everyone is interested.’ These follow-up studies have shown that after a sniff of the hormone, people become more charitable, better at reading emotions on others’ faces and at communicating constructively in arguments. Together, the results fuelled the view that oxytocin universally enhanced the positive aspects of our social nature.

Then, after a few years, contrasting findings began to emerge. Simone Shamay-Tsoory at the University of Haifa, Israel, found that when volunteers played a competitive game, those who inhaled the hormone showed more pleasure when they beat other players, and felt more envy when others won. What’s more, administering oxytocin also has sharply contrasting outcomes depending on a person’s disposition. Jennifer Bartz from Mount Sinai School of Medicine, New York, found that it improves people’s ability to read emotions, but only if they are not very socially adept to begin with. Her research also shows that oxytocin in fact reduces cooperation in subjects who are particularly anxious or sensitive to rejection.

Another discovery is that oxytocin’s effects vary depending on who we are interacting with. Studies conducted by Carolyn DeClerck of the University of Antwerp, Belgium, revealed that people who had received a dose of oxytocin actually became less cooperative when dealing with complete strangers. Meanwhile, Carsten De Dreu at the University of Amsterdam in the Netherlands discovered that volunteers given oxytocin showed favouritism: Dutch men became quicker to associate positive words with Dutch names than with foreign ones, for example. According to De Dreu, oxytocin drives people to care for those in their social circles and defend them from outside dangers. So, it appears that oxytocin strengthens biases, rather than promoting general goodwill, as was previously thought.

There were signs of these subtleties from the start. Bartz has recently shown that in almost half of the existing research results, oxytocin influenced only certain individuals or in certain circumstances. Where once researchers took no notice of such findings, now a more nuanced understanding of oxytocin’s effects is propelling investigations down new lines. To Bartz, the key to understanding what the hormone does lies in pinpointing its core function rather than in cataloguing its seemingly endless effects. There are several hypotheses which are not mutually exclusive. Oxytocin could help to reduce anxiety and fear. Or it could simply motivate people to seek out social connections. She believes that oxytocin acts as a chemical spotlight that shines on social cues – a shift in posture, a flicker of the eyes, a dip in the voice – making people more attuned to their social environment. This would explain why it makes us more likely to look others in the eye and improves our ability to identify emotions. But it could also make things worse for people who are overly sensitive or prone to interpreting social cues in the worst light.

Perhaps we should not be surprised that the oxytocin story has become more perplexing. The hormone is found in everything from octopuses to sheep, and its evolutionary roots stretch back half a billion years. ‘It’s a very simple and ancient molecule that has been co-opted for many different functions,’ says Sue Carter at the University of Illinois, Chicago, USA. ‘It affects primitive parts of the brain like the amygdala, so it’s going to have many effects on just about everything.’ Bartz agrees. ‘Oxytocin probably does some very basic things, but once you add our higher-order thinking and social situations, these basic processes could manifest in different ways depending on individual differences and context.’

Most managers can identify the major trends of the day. But in the course of conducting research in a number of industries and working directly with companies, we have discovered that managers often fail to recognize the less obvious but profound ways these trends are influencing consumers’ aspirations, attitudes, and behaviors. This is especially true of trends that managers view as peripheral to their core markets.

Many ignore trends in their innovation strategies or adopt a wait-and-see approach and let competitors take the lead. At a minimum, such responses mean missed profit opportunities. At the extreme, they can jeopardize a company by ceding to rivals the opportunity to transform the industry. The purpose of this article is twofold: to spur managers to think more expansively about how trends could engender new value propositions in their core markets, and to provide some high-level advice on how to make market research and product development personnel more adept at analyzing and exploiting trends.

One strategy, known as ‘infuse and augment’, is to design a product or service that retains most of the attributes and functions of existing products in the category but adds others that address the needs and desires unleashed by a major trend. Cinnamon is a sweet, fragrant spice produced from the inner bark of trees of the genus Cinnamomum, which is native to the Indian sub-continent. It was known in biblical times, and is mentioned in several books of the Bible, both as an ingredient that was mixed with oils for anointing people’s bodies, and also as a token indicating friendship among lovers and friends. In ancient Rome, mourners attending funerals burnt cinnamon to create a pleasant scent. Most often, however, the spice found its primary use as an additive to food and drink. In the Middle Ages, Europeans who could afford the spice used it to flavour food, particularly meat, and to impress those around them with their ability to purchase an expensive condiment from the ‘exotic’ East. At a banquet, a host would offer guests a plate with various spices piled upon it as a sign of the wealth at his or her disposal. Cinnamon was also reported to have health benefits, and was thought to cure various ailments, such as indigestion.

Toward the end of the Middle Ages, the European middle classes began to desire the lifestyle of the elite, including their consumption of spices. This led to a growth in demand for cinnamon and other spices. At that time, cinnamon was transported by Arab merchants, who closely guarded the secret of the source of the spice from potential rivals. They took it from India, where it was grown, on camels via an overland route to the Mediterranean. Their journey ended when they reached Alexandria. European traders sailed there to purchase their supply of cinnamon, then brought it back to Venice. The spice then travelled from that great trading city to markets all around Europe. Because the overland trade route allowed for only small quantities of the spice to reach Europe, and because Venice had a virtual monopoly of the trade, the Venetians could set the price of cinnamon exorbitantly high. These prices, coupled with the increasing demand, spurred the search for new routes to Asia by Europeans eager to take part in the spice trade.

Seeking the high profits promised by the cinnamon market, Portuguese traders arrived on the island of Ceylon in the Indian Ocean toward the end of the 15th century. Before Europeans arrived on the island, the state had organized the cultivation of cinnamon. People belonging to the ethnic group called the Salagama would peel the bark off young shoots of the cinnamon plant in the rainy season, when the wet bark was more pliable. During the peeling process, they curled the bark into the ‘stick’ shape still associated with the spice today. The Salagama then gave the finished product to the king as a form of tribute. When the Portuguese arrived, they needed to increase production significantly, and so enslaved many other members of the Ceylonese native population, forcing them to work in cinnamon harvesting. In 1518, the Portuguese built a fort on Ceylon, which enabled them to protect the island, so helping them to develop a monopoly in the cinnamon trade and generate very high profits. In the late 16th century, for example, they enjoyed a tenfold profit when shipping cinnamon over a journey of eight days from Ceylon to India.

When the Dutch arrived off the coast of southern Asia at the very beginning of the 17th century, they set their sights on displacing the Portuguese as kings of cinnamon. The Dutch allied themselves with Kandy, an inland kingdom on Ceylon. In return for payments of elephants and cinnamon, they protected the native king from the Portuguese. By 1640, the Dutch broke the 150-year Portuguese monopoly when they overran and occupied their factories. By 1658, they had permanently expelled the Portuguese from the island, thereby gaining control of the lucrative cinnamon trade. In order to protect their hold on the market, the Dutch, like the Portuguese before them, treated the native inhabitants harshly. Because of the need to boost production and satisfy Europe’s ever-increasing appetite for cinnamon, the Dutch began to alter the harvesting practices of the Ceylonese. Over time, the supply of cinnamon trees on the island became nearly exhausted, due to systematic stripping of the bark. Eventually, the Dutch began cultivating their own cinnamon trees to supplement the diminishing number of wild trees available for use.

Then, in 1796, the English arrived on Ceylon, thereby displacing the Dutch from their control of the cinnamon monopoly. By the middle of the 19th century, production of cinnamon reached 1,000 tons a year, after a lower grade quality of the spice became acceptable to European tastes. By that time, cinnamon was being grown in other parts of the Indian Ocean region and in the West Indies, Brazil, and Guyana. Not only was a monopoly of cinnamon becoming impossible, but the spice trade overall was diminishing in economic potential, and was eventually superseded by the rise of trade in coffee, tea, chocolate, and sugar.

At a banquet, a host would offer guests a plate with various spices piled upon it as a sign of the wealth at his or her disposal. Cinnamon was also reported to have health benefits, and was thought to cure various ailments, such as indigestion.

Toward the end of the Middle Ages, the European middle classes began to desire the lifestyle of the elite, including their consumption of spices. This led to a growth in demand for cinnamon and other spices. At that time, cinnamon was transported by Arab merchants, who closely guarded the secret of the source of the spice from potential rivals. They took it from India, where it was grown, on camels via an overland route to the Mediterranean. Their journey ended when they reached Alexandria. European traders sailed there to purchase their supply of cinnamon, then brought it back to Venice. The spice then travelled from that great trading city to markets all around Europe. Because the overland trade route allowed for only small quantities of the spice to reach Europe, and because Venice had a virtual monopoly of the trade, the Venetians could set the price of cinnamon exorbitantly high. These prices, coupled with the increasing demand, spurred the search for new routes to Asia by Europeans eager to take part in the spice trade.

Seeking the high profits promised by the cinnamon market, Portuguese traders arrived on the island of Ceylon in the Indian Ocean toward the end of the 15th century. Before Europeans arrived on the island, the state had organized the cultivation of cinnamon. People belonging to the ethnic group called the Salagama would peel the bark off young shoots of the cinnamon plant in the rainy season, when the wet bark was more pliable. During the peeling process, they curled the bark into the ‘stick’ shape still associated with the spice today. The Salagama then gave the finished product to the king as a form of tribute. When the Portuguese arrived, they needed to increase production significantly, and so enslaved many other members of the Ceylonese native population, forcing them to work in cinnamon harvesting. In 1518, the Portuguese built a fort on Ceylon, which enabled them to protect the island, so helping them to develop a monopoly in the cinnamon trade and generate very high profits. In the late 16th century, for example, they enjoyed a tenfold profit when shipping cinnamon over a journey of eight days from Ceylon to India.

When the Dutch arrived off the coast of southern Asia at the very beginning of the 17th century, they set their sights on displacing the Portuguese as kings of cinnamon. The Dutch allied themselves with Kandy, an inland kingdom on Ceylon. In return for payments of elephants and cinnamon, they protected the native king from the Portuguese. By 1640, the Dutch broke the 150-year Portuguese monopoly when they overran and occupied their factories. By 1658, they had permanently expelled the Portuguese from the island, thereby gaining control of the lucrative cinnamon trade. In order to protect their hold on the market, the Dutch, like the Portuguese before them, treated the native inhabitants harshly. Because of the need to boost production and satisfy Europe’s ever-increasing appetite for cinnamon, the Dutch began to alter the harvesting practices of the Ceylonese. Over time, the supply of cinnamon trees on the island became nearly exhausted, due to systematic stripping of the bark. Eventually, the Dutch began cultivating their own cinnamon trees to supplement the diminishing number of wild trees available for use.

Then, in 1796, the English arrived on Ceylon, thereby displacing the Dutch from their control of the cinnamon monopoly. By the middle of the 19th century, production of cinnamon reached 1,000 tons a year, after a lower grade quality of the spice became acceptable to European tastes. By that time, cinnamon was being grown in other parts of the Indian Ocean region and in the West Indies, Brazil, and Guyana. Not only was a monopoly of cinnamon becoming impossible, but the spice trade overall was diminishing in economic potential, and was eventually superseded by the rise of trade in coffee, tea, chocolate, and sugar.

sentences.text: Cinnamon is a sweet, fragrant spice produced from the inner bark of trees of the genus Cinnamomum, which is native to the Indian sub-continent.
sentences.translation: 肉桂是一种气味芬芳、味道甘甜的香料，由樟属树木的内层树皮制成；这类树木原产于印度次大陆。
sentences.structure: 主干是 Cinnamon is a ... spice；produced... 是过去分词短语修饰 spice，of the genus Cinnamomum 修饰 trees，which 从句说明该属植物的原产地。开篇用“是什么—从哪里来”建立物种与商品身份。

sentences.text: It was known in biblical times, and is mentioned in several books of the Bible, both as an ingredient that was mixed with oils for anointing people’s bodies, and also as a token indicating friendship among lovers and friends.
sentences.translation: 早在《圣经》时代，人们就知道肉桂；《圣经》的多卷书中也提到它：它既是与油混合、用来涂抹人体的配料，也被当作爱侣与朋友之间象征友谊的信物。
sentences.structure: and 连接两个并列谓语 was known 与 is mentioned；both as...and also as... 并列肉桂的两种用途。that was mixed... 修饰 ingredient，for anointing... 表用途，indicating... 修饰 token。两种用途从宗教仪式推进到人际象征。

vocabulary.meaning: 肉桂；本句中的 it 回指该词
以油涂抹身体，常带宗教或仪式含义
象征感情或意图的信物

sentences.text: In ancient Rome, mourners attending funerals burnt cinnamon to create a pleasant scent.
sentences.translation: 在古罗马，参加葬礼的哀悼者会焚烧肉桂，以营造怡人的香气。
sentences.structure: 主干是 mourners burnt cinnamon；attending funerals 是现在分词短语修饰 mourners，to create... 表目的。句子把肉桂从文本记载带入具体仪式场景。

vocabulary.meaning: 肉桂；本句作为焚烧产生香气的材料

sentences.text: Most often, however, the spice found its primary use as an additive to food and drink.
sentences.translation: 不过，肉桂最常见的主要用途还是作为食品和饮料的添加物。
sentences.structure: 主干是 the spice found its primary use as...；Most often 与 however 共同把叙述从仪式用途转回日常用途，as an additive 表明它所充当的角色。

sentences.text: In the Middle Ages, Europeans who could afford the spice used it to flavour food, particularly meat, and to impress those around them with their ability to purchase an expensive condiment from the ‘exotic’ East.
sentences.translation: 中世纪时，买得起这种香料的欧洲人用它给食物调味，尤其是肉类；他们还借自己有能力购买来自“异域”东方的昂贵调味品，给周围的人留下深刻印象。
sentences.structure: 主干是 Europeans used it... and to impress...；who could afford... 修饰 Europeans，两个 to 不定式并列说明实用与炫示用途，with their ability... 交代留下印象的手段。引号中的 exotic 暗示欧洲人的异域想象。

vocabulary.meaning: 异域的；带陌生、新奇色彩

sentences.text: At a banquet, a host would offer guests a plate with various spices piled upon it as a sign of the wealth at his or her disposal.
sentences.translation: 在宴会上，主人会给宾客端上一只盘子，盘中堆放着各种香料，以此显示自己可支配的财富。
sentences.structure: 主干是 a host would offer guests a plate；with... 是介词短语修饰 plate，piled upon it 是过去分词短语修饰 spices，as a sign of... 表示展示目的。香料从调味品变成财富的可视化符号。

vocabulary.meaning: 香料；本句复数指宴席上陈列的多种香料

sentences.text: Cinnamon was also reported to have health benefits, and was thought to cure various ailments, such as indigestion.
sentences.translation: 据说肉桂还有益健康，并被认为可以治疗各种病症，例如消化不良。
sentences.structure: 两个被动谓语 was reported 与 was thought 并列；to have 与 to cure 分别承接报道和看法，such as 引出具体病症。被动结构保留了历史说法的距离，并不把疗效写成现代事实。

sentences.text: Toward the end of the Middle Ages, the European middle classes began to desire the lifestyle of the elite, including their consumption of spices.
sentences.translation: 临近中世纪末期，欧洲中产阶层开始向往精英阶层的生活方式，其中也包括他们消费香料的习惯。
sentences.structure: 主干是 the European middle classes began to desire...；Toward... 给时间背景，including... 补充精英生活方式的具体内容。本段由身份模仿引出需求增长。

vocabulary.meaning: 香料；本句用复数概括精英消费品

sentences.text: This led to a growth in demand for cinnamon and other spices.
sentences.translation: 这导致肉桂及其他香料的需求增长。
sentences.structure: 主干是 This led to...；This 回指中产阶层模仿精英消费，a growth in demand 把社会欲望转化为市场结果。

vocabulary.meaning: 香料；本句指肉桂之外的其他香料

sentences.text: At that time, cinnamon was transported by Arab merchants, who closely guarded the secret of the source of the spice from potential rivals.
sentences.translation: 当时，肉桂由阿拉伯商人运输；他们严密守护香料来源的秘密，不让潜在竞争对手得知。
sentences.structure: 主干是 cinnamon was transported...；who 非限制性定语从句补充 merchants 的保密策略，guard...from... 表示防止竞争者获取秘密。供应链信息不透明为欧洲寻找新路线埋下伏笔。

sentences.text: They took it from India, where it was grown, on camels via an overland route to the Mediterranean.
sentences.translation: 他们从印度取得肉桂——肉桂就种植在那里——再用骆驼沿陆路运到地中海。
sentences.structure: 主干是 They took it from India...to the Mediterranean；where 从句说明产地，on camels 表运输工具，via an overland route 表路线。多个介词短语依次画出供应链。

vocabulary.meaning: 肉桂；本句中的 it 回指前句的 cinnamon
骆驼；本句复数作运输工具

sentences.text: Their journey ended when they reached Alexandria.
sentences.translation: 他们抵达亚历山大港时，这段旅程便告结束。
sentences.structure: 主干是 Their journey ended；when 从句说明终点时刻。短句把印度至地中海的陆路运输落在一个明确节点上。

vocabulary.meaning: 旅程；本句指陆路运输过程

sentences.text: European traders sailed there to purchase their supply of cinnamon, then brought it back to Venice.
sentences.translation: 欧洲商人航行到那里采购肉桂货源，然后把肉桂运回威尼斯。
sentences.structure: 主干是 traders sailed...then brought...；to purchase 表航行目的，there 回指 Alexandria，it 回指 cinnamon。句子接续陆路之后的海运环节。

sentences.text: The spice then travelled from that great trading city to markets all around Europe.
sentences.translation: 随后，这种香料从那座重要的贸易城市流向欧洲各地的市场。
sentences.structure: 主干是 The spice travelled from...to...；that great trading city 回指 Venice，空间路径把威尼斯写成欧洲分销枢纽。

sentences.text: Because the overland trade route allowed for only small quantities of the spice to reach Europe, and because Venice had a virtual monopoly of the trade, the Venetians could set the price of cinnamon exorbitantly high.
sentences.translation: 由于陆路贸易路线只能让少量香料抵达欧洲，加之威尼斯实际上垄断了这项贸易，威尼斯人便能把肉桂价格定得高得惊人。
sentences.structure: 两个 because 从句并列给出“供给少”和“垄断”两项原因；主句 the Venetians could set... 写定价结果。allow for 在这里表示容许某种数量通过，不是“考虑到”。

vocabulary.meaning: 香料；本句指进入欧洲的肉桂
高得离谱地；过分昂贵地

sentences.text: These prices, coupled with the increasing demand, spurred the search for new routes to Asia by Europeans eager to take part in the spice trade.
sentences.translation: 这样的高价，再加上不断增长的需求，推动了欧洲人寻找通往亚洲的新路线；他们迫切希望参与香料贸易。
sentences.structure: 主干是 These prices spurred the search；coupled with... 是过去分词插入语补充共同原因，by Europeans 说明寻找者，eager... 修饰 Europeans。价格与需求共同把贸易史推向航海扩张。

sentences.text: Seeking the high profits promised by the cinnamon market, Portuguese traders arrived on the island of Ceylon in the Indian Ocean toward the end of the 15th century.
sentences.translation: 为了追逐肉桂市场所许诺的高额利润，葡萄牙商人在15世纪末来到印度洋的锡兰岛。
sentences.structure: Seeking... 是现在分词短语表示动机，promised by... 修饰 profits；主干 Portuguese traders arrived...。利润诱因把欧洲人的“寻找路线”落实为抵达产地。

vocabulary.meaning: 贸易商；本句指葡萄牙商人

sentences.text: Before Europeans arrived on the island, the state had organized the cultivation of cinnamon.
sentences.translation: 欧洲人抵达该岛之前，当地政权已经组织起肉桂种植。
sentences.structure: Before 从句给时间界线；主句用过去完成时 had organized，强调欧洲人到来前已有制度化生产。

vocabulary.meaning: 国家或政权；本句指当地统治机构

sentences.text: People belonging to the ethnic group called the Salagama would peel the bark off young shoots of the cinnamon plant in the rainy season, when the wet bark was more pliable.
sentences.translation: 属于萨拉伽马族群的人会在雨季从肉桂植株的嫩枝上剥下树皮，因为那时湿润的树皮更柔韧易弯。
sentences.structure: 主干是 People would peel...；belonging... 与 called... 逐层修饰 People 和 ethnic group，when 从句说明选择雨季的原因。would 表过去的惯常做法。

sentences.text: During the peeling process, they curled the bark into the ‘stick’ shape still associated with the spice today.
sentences.translation: 在剥皮过程中，他们把树皮卷成“棒状”；直到今天，人们仍把这种形状与肉桂联系在一起。
sentences.structure: 主干是 they curled the bark into...；still associated... 是过去分词短语修饰 shape。句子解释肉桂棒的外形如何由加工动作形成，并连接古今。

vocabulary.meaning: 树皮；本句再次指被加工的原料

sentences.text: The Salagama then gave the finished product to the king as a form of tribute.
sentences.translation: 随后，萨拉伽马人把制成品交给国王，作为一种贡品。
sentences.structure: 主干是 The Salagama gave the finished product to the king；as a form of tribute 说明交付的制度性质，从生产流程转向权力关系。

sentences.text: When the Portuguese arrived, they needed to increase production significantly, and so enslaved many other members of the Ceylonese native population, forcing them to work in cinnamon harvesting.
sentences.translation: 葡萄牙人到来后，需要大幅提高产量，于是奴役了许多其他锡兰原住民，强迫他们从事肉桂采收。
sentences.structure: When 从句给时间背景；主句并列 needed 与 enslaved，and so 明示因果；forcing... 是现在分词短语补充奴役的结果。句子把利润扩张与强制劳动直接连接。

sentences.text: In 1518, the Portuguese built a fort on Ceylon, which enabled them to protect the island, so helping them to develop a monopoly in the cinnamon trade and generate very high profits.
sentences.translation: 1518年，葡萄牙人在锡兰修建了一座堡垒；这使他们能够保护该岛，进而帮助他们在肉桂贸易中建立垄断并获取极高利润。
sentences.structure: 主干是 the Portuguese built a fort；which 从句说明堡垒的功能，so helping... 表由此产生的进一步结果，develop 与 generate 并列。句子写军事设施如何转化为市场控制。

vocabulary.meaning: 葡萄牙人；本句为修建堡垒并建立垄断的一方

sentences.text: In the late 16th century, for example, they enjoyed a tenfold profit when shipping cinnamon over a journey of eight days from Ceylon to India.
sentences.translation: 例如，在16世纪后期，他们把肉桂从锡兰运往印度，八天航程便能获得十倍利润。
sentences.structure: 主干是 they enjoyed a tenfold profit；when shipping... 是省略主语的时间状语，over a journey of eight days 补充航程长度。tenfold 用一个数字压缩出贸易暴利。

vocabulary.meaning: 利润；本句再次写贸易收益
旅程；本句指八天运输航程

sentences.text: When the Dutch arrived off the coast of southern Asia at the very beginning of the 17th century, they set their sights on displacing the Portuguese as kings of cinnamon.
sentences.translation: 17世纪刚开始时，荷兰人抵达南亚近海，便立志取代葡萄牙人，成为肉桂贸易的霸主。
sentences.structure: When 从句给出新竞争者登场的时间与地点；主干 they set their sights on...，displacing... 是介词 on 的宾语，as kings of cinnamon 写取代后的目标身份。该比喻把商业竞争写成争夺王位。

vocabulary.meaning: 肉桂；本句代指肉桂贸易

sentences.text: The Dutch allied themselves with Kandy, an inland kingdom on Ceylon.
sentences.translation: 荷兰人与康提结盟；康提是锡兰的一个内陆王国。
sentences.structure: 主干是 The Dutch allied themselves with Kandy；逗号后的 an inland kingdom... 是同位语解释 Kandy。短句交代荷兰挑战葡萄牙的本地联盟。

sentences.text: In return for payments of elephants and cinnamon, they protected the native king from the Portuguese.
sentences.translation: 作为获得大象和肉桂报酬的回报，他们保护当地国王免受葡萄牙人侵害。
sentences.structure: In return for... 前置说明交换条件；主干 they protected the native king from...。句子揭示联盟是一项物资与军事保护的交易。

vocabulary.meaning: 葡萄牙人；本句为保护所针对的一方

sentences.text: By 1640, the Dutch broke the 150-year Portuguese monopoly when they overran and occupied their factories.
sentences.translation: 到1640年，荷兰人攻占葡萄牙人的工厂，打破了葡萄牙长达150年的垄断。
sentences.structure: 主干是 the Dutch broke...monopoly；when 从句说明打破垄断的具体行动，overran 与 occupied 并列。时间数字突出垄断持续之久。

vocabulary.meaning: 葡萄牙的；本句修饰 monopoly

sentences.text: By 1658, they had permanently expelled the Portuguese from the island, thereby gaining control of the lucrative cinnamon trade.
sentences.translation: 到1658年，他们已经把葡萄牙人永久逐出该岛，从而控制了利润丰厚的肉桂贸易。
sentences.structure: 主句用过去完成时 had expelled 表示到1658年已完成；thereby gaining... 是现在分词结果状语，说明驱逐带来的贸易控制。

sentences.text: In order to protect their hold on the market, the Dutch, like the Portuguese before them, treated the native inhabitants harshly.
sentences.translation: 为了保住对市场的控制，荷兰人像此前的葡萄牙人一样，残酷对待当地居民。
sentences.structure: In order to... 表目的；the Dutch 是主语，like... 是插入比较，主干落在 treated...harshly。比较结构强调统治者更换，但压迫方式延续。

sentences.text: Because of the need to boost production and satisfy Europe’s ever-increasing appetite for cinnamon, the Dutch began to alter the harvesting practices of the Ceylonese.
sentences.translation: 由于需要提高产量并满足欧洲对肉桂日益增长的强烈需求，荷兰人开始改变锡兰人的采收方式。
sentences.structure: Because of... 给出原因，其中 boost 与 satisfy 并列；主干 the Dutch began to alter...。appetite 把市场需求人格化为越吃越大的胃口。

vocabulary.meaning: 对……的强烈需求；字面义为食欲

sentences.text: Over time, the supply of cinnamon trees on the island became nearly exhausted, due to systematic stripping of the bark.
sentences.translation: 随着时间推移，由于持续而系统地剥取树皮，岛上的肉桂树资源几乎枯竭。
sentences.structure: 主干是 the supply...became nearly exhausted；Over time 写渐变过程，due to... 给直接原因。被动式 exhausted 把生产扩张的生态后果放到句子中心。

sentences.text: Eventually, the Dutch began cultivating their own cinnamon trees to supplement the diminishing number of wild trees available for use.
sentences.translation: 最终，荷兰人开始自行栽培肉桂树，以补充数量日益减少、可供利用的野生树木。
sentences.structure: 主干是 the Dutch began cultivating...；to supplement... 表目的，diminishing 与 available for use 都修饰 wild trees。此句写资源枯竭迫使垄断者转向人工栽培。

sentences.text: Then, in 1796, the English arrived on Ceylon, thereby displacing the Dutch from their control of the cinnamon monopoly.
sentences.translation: 随后在1796年，英国人抵达锡兰，从而取代荷兰人，夺走了他们对肉桂垄断贸易的控制。
sentences.structure: 主干是 the English arrived...；thereby displacing... 是结果状语，from their control... 说明荷兰人被排挤出的位置。叙事再次用“新来者—取代旧霸主”推进权力更迭。

sentences.text: By the middle of the 19th century, production of cinnamon reached 1,000 tons a year, after a lower grade quality of the spice became acceptable to European tastes.
sentences.translation: 到19世纪中叶，在较低等级的肉桂也开始为欧洲人口味所接受之后，肉桂年产量达到了1,000吨。
sentences.structure: 主干是 production...reached...；By... 给时间界线，after 从句解释产量扩大的市场条件。原文保留 lower grade quality 这一不寻常搭配，译文不擅自改写事实。

sentences.text: By that time, cinnamon was being grown in other parts of the Indian Ocean region and in the West Indies, Brazil, and Guyana.
sentences.translation: 到那时，印度洋地区其他地方，以及西印度群岛、巴西和圭亚那，也都开始种植肉桂。
sentences.structure: 主干是 cinnamon was being grown...，过去进行时被动强调当时扩散中的种植活动；两个 in 短语并列列出新产区。产地扩张削弱了单一来源的控制。

sentences.text: Not only was a monopoly of cinnamon becoming impossible, but the spice trade overall was diminishing in economic potential, and was eventually superseded by the rise of trade in coffee, tea, chocolate, and sugar.
sentences.translation: 不仅肉桂垄断已变得不可能，整个香料贸易的经济潜力也在下降，并最终被咖啡、茶、巧克力和糖贸易的兴起所取代。

readingSections.title: Reading Passage 2
readingSections.subtitle: The positive and negative effects of the chemical known as the ‘love hormone’
paragraphs: Oxytocin is a chemical, a hormone produced in the pituitary gland in the brain. It was through various studies focusing on animals that scientists first became aware of the influence of oxytocin. They discovered that it helps reinforce the bonds between prairie voles, which mate for life, and triggers the motherly behaviour that sheep show towards their newborn lambs. It is also released by women in childbirth, strengthening the attachment between mother and baby. Few chemicals have as positive a reputation as oxytocin, which is sometimes referred to as the ‘love hormone’. One sniff of it can, it is claimed, make a person more trusting, empathetic, generous and cooperative. It is time, however, to revise this wholly optimistic view. A new wave of studies has shown that its effects vary greatly depending on the person and the circumstances, and it can impact on our social interactions for worse as well as for better.

Oxytocin’s role in human behaviour first emerged in 2005. In a groundbreaking experiment, Markus Heinrichs and his colleagues at the University of Freiburg, Germany, asked volunteers to do an activity in which they could invest money with an anonymous person who was not guaranteed to be honest. The team found that participants who had sniffed oxytocin via a nasal spray beforehand invested more money than those who received a placebo instead. The study was the start of research into the effects of oxytocin on human interactions. ‘For eight years, it was quite a lonesome field,’ Heinrichs recalls. ‘Now, everyone is interested.’ These follow-up studies have shown that after a sniff of the hormone, people become more charitable, better at reading emotions on others’ faces and at communicating constructively in arguments. Together, the results fuelled the view that oxytocin universally enhanced the positive aspects of our social nature.

Then, after a few years, contrasting findings began to emerge. Simone Shamay-Tsoory at the University of Haifa, Israel, found that when volunteers played a competitive game, those who inhaled the hormone showed more pleasure when they beat other players, and felt more envy when others won. What’s more, administering oxytocin also has sharply contrasting outcomes depending on a person’s disposition. Jennifer Bartz from Mount Sinai School of Medicine, New York, found that it improves people’s ability to read emotions, but only if they are not very socially adept to begin with. Her research also shows that oxytocin in fact reduces cooperation in subjects who are particularly anxious or sensitive to rejection.

Another discovery is that oxytocin’s effects vary depending on who we are interacting with. Studies conducted by Carolyn DeClerck of the University of Antwerp, Belgium, revealed that people who had received a dose of oxytocin actually became less cooperative when dealing with complete strangers. Meanwhile, Carsten De Dreu at the University of Amsterdam in the Netherlands discovered that volunteers given oxytocin showed favouritism: Dutch men became quicker to associate positive words with Dutch names than with foreign ones, for example. According to De Dreu, oxytocin drives people to care for those in their social circles and defend them from outside dangers. So, it appears that oxytocin strengthens biases, rather than promoting general goodwill, as was previously thought.

There were signs of these subtleties from the start. Bartz has recently shown that in almost half of the existing research results, oxytocin influenced only certain individuals or in certain circumstances. Where once researchers took no notice of such findings, now a more nuanced understanding of oxytocin’s effects is propelling investigations down new lines. To Bartz, the key to understanding what the hormone does lies in pinpointing its core function rather than in cataloguing its seemingly endless effects. There are several hypotheses which are not mutually exclusive. Oxytocin could help to reduce anxiety and fear. Or it could simply motivate people to seek out social connections. She believes that oxytocin acts as a chemical spotlight that shines on social cues – a shift in posture, a flicker of the eyes, a dip in the voice – making people more attuned to their social environment. This would explain why it makes us more likely to look others in the eye and improves our ability to identify emotions. But it could also make things worse for people who are overly sensitive or prone to interpreting social cues in the worst light.

Perhaps we should not be surprised that the oxytocin story has become more perplexing. The hormone is found in everything from octopuses to sheep, and its evolutionary roots stretch back half a billion years. ‘It’s a very simple and ancient molecule that has been co-opted for many different functions,’ says Sue Carter at the University of Illinois, Chicago, USA. ‘It affects primitive parts of the brain like the amygdala, so it’s going to have many effects on just about everything.’ Bartz agrees. ‘Oxytocin probably does some very basic things, but once you add our higher-order thinking and social situations, these basic processes could manifest in different ways depending on individual differences and context.’

readingSections.title: Reading Passage 3
readingSections.subtitle: Experts from Harvard Business School give advice to managers
paragraphs: Most managers can identify the major trends of the day. But in the course of conducting research in a number of industries and working directly with companies, we have discovered that managers often fail to recognize the less obvious but profound ways these trends are influencing consumers’ aspirations, attitudes, and behaviors. This is especially true of trends that managers view as peripheral to their core markets.

Many ignore trends in their innovation strategies or adopt a wait-and-see approach and let competitors take the lead. At a minimum, such responses mean missed profit opportunities. At the extreme, they can jeopardize a company by ceding to rivals the opportunity to transform the industry. The purpose of this article is twofold: to spur managers to think more expansively about how trends could engender new value propositions in their core markets, and to provide some high-level advice on how to make market research and product development personnel more adept at analyzing and exploiting trends.

One strategy, known as ‘infuse and augment’, is to design a product or service that retains most of the attributes and functions of existing products in the category but adds others that address the needs and desires unleashed by a major trend. A case in point is the Poppy range of handbags, which the firm Coach created in response to the economic downturn of 2008. The Coach brand had been a symbol of opulence and luxury for nearly 70 years, and the most obvious reaction to the downturn would have been to lower prices. However, that would have risked cheapening the brand’s image. Instead, they initiated a consumer-research project which revealed that customers were eager to lift themselves and the country out of tough times. Using these insights, Coach launched the lower-priced Poppy handbags, which were in vibrant colors, and looked more youthful and playful than conventional Coach products. Creating the sub-brand allowed Coach to avert an across-the-board price cut. In contrast to the many companies that responded to the recession by cutting prices, Coach saw the new consumer mindset as an opportunity for innovation and renewal.

A further example of this strategy was supermarket Tesco’s response to consumers’ growing concerns about the environment. With that in mind, Tesco, one of the world’s top five retailers, introduced its Greener Living program, which demonstrates the company’s commitment to protecting the environment by involving consumers in ways that produce tangible results. For example, Tesco customers can accumulate points for such activities as reusing bags, recycling cans and printer cartridges, and buying home-insulation materials. Like points earned on regular purchases, these green points can be redeemed for cash. Tesco has not abandoned its traditional retail offerings but augmented its business with these innovations, thereby infusing its value proposition with a green streak.

A more radical strategy is ‘combine and transcend’. This entails combining aspects of the product’s existing value proposition with attributes addressing changes arising from a trend, to create a novel experience – one that may land the company in an entirely new market space. At first glance, spending resources to incorporate elements of a seemingly irrelevant trend into one’s core offerings sounds like it’s hardly worthwhile. But consider Nike’s move to integrate the digital revolution into its reputation for high-performance athletic footwear. In 2006, they teamed up with technology company Apple to launch Nike+, a digital sports kit comprising a sensor that attaches to the running shoe and a wireless receiver that connects to the user’s iPod. By combining Nike’s original value proposition for amateur athletes with one for digital consumers, the Nike+ sports kit and web interface moved the company from a focus on athletic apparel to a new plane of engagement with its customers.

A third approach, known as ‘counteract and reaffirm’, involves developing products or services that stress the values traditionally associated with the category in ways that allow consumers to oppose – or at least temporarily escape from – the aspects of trends they view as undesirable. A product that accomplished this is the ME2, a video game created by Canada’s iToys. By reaffirming the toy category’s association with physical play, the ME2 counteracted some of the widely perceived negative impacts of digital gaming devices. Like other handheld games, the device featured a host of exciting interactive games, a full-color LCD screen, and advanced 3D graphics. What set it apart was that it incorporated the traditional physical component of children’s play: it contained a pedometer, which tracked and awarded points for physical activity (walking, running, biking, skateboarding, climbing stairs). The child could use the points to enhance various virtual skills needed for the video game. The ME2, introduced in mid-2008, catered to kids’ huge desire to play video games while countering the negatives, such as associations with lack of exercise and obesity.

Once you have gained perspective on how trend-related changes in consumer opinions and behaviors impact on your category, you can determine which of our three innovation strategies to pursue. When your category’s basic value proposition continues to be meaningful for consumers influenced by the trend, the infuse-and-augment strategy will allow you to reinvigorate the category. If analysis reveals an increasing disparity between your category and consumers’ new focus, your innovations need to transcend the category to integrate the two worlds. Finally, if aspects of the category clash with undesired outcomes of a trend, such as associations with unhealthy lifestyles, there is an opportunity to counteract those changes by reaffirming the core values of your category.

Trends – technological, economic, environmental, social, or political – that affect how people perceive the world around them and shape what they expect from products and services present firms with unique opportunities for growth.

questionSections.summary:
The earliest findings about oxytocin and bonding came from research involving 21 __________. It was also discovered that humans produce oxytocin during 22 __________. An experiment in 2005, in which participants were given either oxytocin or a 23 __________, reinforced the belief that the hormone had a positive effect.
However, later research suggests that this is not always the case. A study at the University of Haifa where participants took part in a 24 __________, revealed the negative emotions which oxytocin can trigger. A study at the University of Antwerp showed people’s lack of willingness to help 25 __________ while under the influence of oxytocin. Meanwhile, research at the University of Amsterdam revealed that people who have been given oxytocin consider 26 __________ that are familiar to them in their own country to have more positive associations than those from other cultures.
questionSections.summaryZh:
关于催产素与情感联结的最早发现来自涉及21____的研究。研究还发现，人类在22____期间会产生催产素。2005年的一项实验给参与者使用催产素或23____，强化了该激素具有积极作用的看法。
然而，后来的研究表明，情况并非总是如此。海法大学的一项研究让参与者参加一场24____，揭示了催产素可能触发的负面情绪。安特卫普大学的一项研究显示，人在催产素影响下不愿帮助25____。与此同时，阿姆斯特丹大学的研究发现，使用催产素的人认为本国熟悉的26____比其他文化中的对应事物具有更积极的联想。
